¶
The velocities in different gases may be compared by this apparatus by filling the dust-tube with the gases in place of air. If <math>\text{L}_1</math> is the internodal distance and <math>\text{U}_1</math> the velocity in a gas, <math>\text{L}</math> and <math>\text{U}</math> being the corresponding values for air, we have <math>\text{U}_1/\text{U} = \text{L}_1/\text{L}</math>.

'''''Specific Heats' Ratio.''''' Kundt's dust-tube may also be employed for the determination of the ratio of the specific heats of a gas or vapour. If <math>\text{U}</math> is the velocity of sound in a gas at pressure <math>\text{P}</math> with density <math>\rho</math>, and if waves of length <math>\lambda</math> and frequency <math>\text{N}</math> are propagated through it, then the distance between the dust-heaps is
{{block center|<math>d = \frac{\lambda}{2} = \frac{\text{U}}{2\text{N}} = \frac{1}{2\text{N}}\sqrt{\frac{\gamma\text{P}}{\rho}},</math>}}
where <math>\gamma</math> is the ratio of the two specific heats. If <math>d</math> is measured for two gases in succession for the same frequency <math>\text{N}</math>, we have
{{block center|<math>\frac{\gamma_2}{\gamma_1} = \frac{\rho_2\text{P}_1}{\rho_1\text{P}_2}\ \frac{d_2{}^2}{d_1{}^2},</math>}}
where the suffixes denote the gases to which the quantities relate. If <math>\gamma_1</math> is known this gives <math>\gamma_2</math>. Kundt and Warburg applied the method to find <math>\gamma</math> for mercury vapour (''Pogg. Ann.'', 1876, 157, p. 356), using a double form of the apparatus in which there are two dust-tubes worked by the same sounding rod. This rod is supported at <math>\tfrac{1}{4}</math> and <math>\tfrac{3}{4}</math> of its length where it enters the two dust-tubes, as represented diagrammatically in fig. 32. It is stroked in the middle so as to
readings.c1s6:
excite its second mode of vibration. The method ensures that the two frequencies shall be exactly the same. In the mercury experiment the sounding rod was sealed into the dust-tube, which was exhausted of air, and contained only some mercury and some quartz dust to give the heaps. It was placed in a high temperature oven, where the mercury was evaporated. The second tube containing air was outside. When a known temperature was attained the sounder was excited, and <math>d_2</math> and <math>d_1</math> could be measured. From the temperature, <math>\text{P}_2/\rho_2</math> was known, and <math>\gamma_2/\gamma_1</math> could then be found. Taking <math>\gamma_1 = 1{\cdot}41</math>, <math>\gamma_2</math> was determined to be 1·66. Lord Rayleigh and Sir William Ramsay (''Phil. Trans.'' A. 1895, pt. i. p. 187) also used a single dust-tube with a sounder to find <math>\gamma</math> for argon, and again the value was 1·66.

'''''Amplitude of Vibration.''''' Determinations of the pressure changes, or extent of excursion of the air, in sounding organ pipes have been made by A. Kundt (''Pogg. Ann.'', 1868, 134, p. 163), A. J. I. Töpler and L. Boltzmann (''Pogg. Ann.'', vol. 141, or Rayleigh, ''Sound'', ii. § 422''a''), and E. Mach (''Optisch-akustischen Versuche'', 1873). Mach's method is perhaps the most direct. The pipe was fixed in a horizontal position, and along the top wall ran a platinum wire wetted with sulphuric acid. When the wire was heated by an electric current a fine line of vapour descended from each drop. The pipe was closed at the centre by a membrane which prevented a through draught, yet permitted the vibrations, as it was at a node. The vapour line, therefore, merely vibrated to and fro when the pipe was sounded. The extent of vibration at different parts of the pipe was studied through a glass side wall, a stroboscopic method being used to get the position of the vapour line at a definite part of the vibration. Mach found an excursion of 0·4 cm. at the end of an open pipe 123 cm. long. The amplitude found by the other observers was of the same order. For the vibration of air in other cavities than long cylindrical pipes we refer to Rayleigh's ''Sound'', vol. ii. chs. 12 and 16.

''Propagation of Waves in Pipes of Circular Section.''—Helmholtz investigated the velocity of propagation of sound in pipes, taking into account the viscosity of the air (Rayleigh, ''Sound'', ii. § 347), and Kirchhoff investigated it, taking into account both the viscosity and the heat communication between the air and the walls of the pipe (''loc. cit.'' ii. § 350). Both obtained the value for the velocity
{{block center|<math>\text{U}\left(1-\frac{\text{C}}{\text{R}\sqrt{2\pi\text{N}\rho}}\right),</math>}}

¶
Let <math>\text{AB}</math> (fig. 33) represent the string with the ends <math>\text{AB}</math> fixed. Let a disturbance once set going travel along unchanged in form from <math>\text{A}</math> to <math>\text{B}</math> with velocity <math>\text{U}</math>. Then move <math>\text{AB}</math> from right to left with this velocity, and the disturbance remains fixed in space. Take a point <math>\text{P}</math> in the disturbed part, and a point <math>\text{Q}</math> which the disturbance has not yet reached. Since the conditions in the region <math>\text{PQ}</math> remain always the same, the momentum perpendicular to <math>\text{AB}</math> entering the region at <math>\text{Q}</math> is equal to the momentum perpendicular to <math>\text{AB}</math> leaving the region at <math>\text{P}</math>. But, since the motion at <math>\text{Q}</math> is along <math>\text{AB}</math>, there is no momentum there perpendicular to <math>\text{AB}</math>. So also there is on the whole none in that direction leaving at <math>\text{P}</math>. Let the tangent at <math>\text{P}</math> make angle <math>\phi</math> with <math>\text{AB}</math>. The velocity of the string at <math>\text{P}</math> parallel to <math>\text{PM}</math> is <math>\text{U} \sin \phi</math>, and the mass of string passing <math>\text{P}</math> is <math>m\text{U}</math> per second, so that <math>m\text{U}^2 \sin \phi</math> is carried out per second. But the tension at <math>\text{P}</math> is <math>\text{T}</math>, parallel to the tangent, and <math>\text{T} \sin \phi</math> parallel to <math>\text{PM}</math>, and through this <math>-\text{T} \sin \phi</math> is the momentum passing out at <math>\text{P}</math> per second. Since the resultant is zero, <math>m\text{U}^2 \sin \phi - \text{T} \sin \phi = 0</math>, or <math>\text{U}^2 = \text{T}/m</math>.

Now keep <math>\text{AB}</math> fixed, and the disturbance travels with velocity <math>\text{U}</math>. We might make this investigation more general by introducing a force <math>\text{X}</math> as in the investigation for air, but it hardly appears necessary.

To form stationary waves two equal trains must be able to travel in opposite directions with equal velocities, and to be superposed. We must show then that the force called out by the sum of the disturbances is equal to the sum of the forces called out by each train separately.

In order that the velocity shall remain unchanged the tension <math>\text{T}</math> must remain the same. This implies that the disturbance is so small that the length is not appreciably altered. The component of <math>\text{T}</math>
